newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland Bank sees risks of accelerating inflation.
newsitem.headline: Finland Bank sees risks of accelerating inflation.

text.p: The Bank of Finland said on Monday that the risks of accelerating inflation had increased and that although there was no reason to change monetary policy now, a tightening would have to be considered if the likelihood of quicker inflation grew.

The Finnish central bank, in a statement with the release of its quarterly Markka & Talous (Markka and the Economy) publication, said it expected underlying inflation to accelerate to slightly over two percent in 1998.
"Due to the rise in housing prices the rise of the consumer price index will be quicker," it said.
The Bank's stated monetary policy target is for a core inflation rate of no more than about two percent year-on-year.
"Although the inflation trend has so far remained calm, the risks of accelerating inflation have increased," the Bank of Finland said.

"While the current outlook does not portend a change in the stance of monetary policy, an increase in the probability that inflation will exceed the forecasted rate would force the central bank to consider monetary tightening,"
"If the likelihood of quicker than forecast inflation grows a tightening of monetary policy must be considered," it added.
Finlands's brisk economic growth -- forecast at 4-5 percent this year, or double the pace expected for most EU countries -- threatened to upset price stability, the central bank said.
"Production and labour bottlenecks in certain sectors may boost inflation expectations," it said.
That in turn could influence pricing behaviour also in sectors not subject to bottlenecks, the central bank said.

A "key element" behind the forecast of 1998 core inflation at slightly over two percent was "the assumption that next year's pay settlements will be moderate and consistent with low inflation and that wage drift will remain subdued," it said.
The Bank of Finland said the moderate nominal wage hikes of the past two years had contributed to the fall in interest rates and to the stability of monetary conditions.
For growth and improving employment it would be crucial that this kind of "balanced performance" continued, it said. @
